target: Ojalá haga buen tiempo este fin de semana.
english: I hope the weather is nice this weekend.
tip: 'Ojalá' is fossilized Arabic – 'law sha Allah', if God wills. It's a leftover prayer, so it always takes subjunctive: 'ojalá haga', never 'hace'.

target: Abro la ventana para que entre aire fresco.
english: I open the window to let in fresh air.
tip: Para + infinitive only works when subjects match. New actor doing the goal? Switch to 'para que' + subjunctive: the air, not you, does the entering – 'para que entre'.

target: Busco un vuelo que salga por la mañana.
english: I'm looking for a flight that leaves in the morning.
tip: 'Salga', not 'sale' – this flight may not exist yet. Hunting for something unfound? Its description takes subjunctive. A found flight 'que sale' would be indicative.

target: Este fin de semana nos toca limpiar la casa.
english: It's our turn to clean the house this weekend.
tip: 'Tocar' (to touch) doubles as 'to be one's turn': the chore touches you. 'Nos toca limpiar' – cleaning lands on us. The task is the subject; you're just its target.

target: Se comenta que van a abrir un nuevo restaurante.
english: They say a new restaurant is going to open.
tip: Se comenta = 'it's being said' – the se erases the speaker entirely. Spanish's favorite way to pass along gossip without naming who's talking.

target: ¿Se la has enviado ya? Lleva esperándola toda la semana.
english: Have you sent it to her already? She's been waiting for it all week.
tip: 'Lleva esperándola' – she 'carries' waiting? Llevar + -ndo measures how long something has been going on: carrying a whole week of waiting, no 'has been' needed.

target: Antes de que los niños lleguen, quiero tener la casa limpia.
english: Before the kids arrive, I want to have the house clean.
tip: Antes de que always takes subjunctive: lleguen.

target: Es mejor que lleguemos temprano.
english: It's better that we arrive early.
tip: Es mejor que is a judgment, not a fact – so lleguemos goes subjunctive. Arriving early is being recommended, not reported as actually happening.

target: El proyecto me lo explicó María.
english: María explained the project to me.
tip: 'El proyecto' comes first for emphasis – but front an object and Spanish demands an echo pronoun: that 'lo' re-marks the project so nobody reads it as the subject.

target: Le pasa algo, está muy callada.
english: Something's wrong with her, she's very quiet.
tip: "Pasar" for what's happening: "¿Qué te pasa?" = What's wrong with you? / What's happening to you? Indirect object marks the affected person.

target: Ve al supermercado y compra leche.
english: Go to the supermarket and buy milk.
tip: Ve here is 'go!' (from ir) – but ve is also the command for ver, 'see!'. Only context decides which; the supermarket destination settles it here.

target: Necesito que me envíes el archivo.
english: I need you to send me the file.
tip: Necesitar que + subjunctive: needing someone else to act. "Necesito que me ayudes" (I need you to help me).

target: Sigo sin encontrar mi tarjeta de embarque.
english: I still can't find my boarding pass.
tip: Seguir sin + infinitive = still haven't / still can't.

target: Haga lo que haga, nunca parece suficiente.
english: Whatever he does, it never seems enough.
tip: 'Haga lo que haga' is literally 'may he do what he may do' – twin subjunctives sandwiching lo que is Spanish's formula for 'whatever / no matter what'.

target: Ponte el abrigo, que fuera hace frío.
english: Put on your coat, it's cold outside.
tip: 'El abrigo', not 'tu abrigo' – with clothes and body parts, the reflexive 'ponte' already says whose it is, so Spanish uses plain 'el' where English insists on 'your'.

target: Trae una chaqueta por si hace frío.
english: Bring a jacket in case it's cold.
tip: 'Por si' (in case) skips the subjunctive you'd expect: plain 'hace', not 'haga'. Spanish treats the just-in-case scenario as real enough to state flatly.

target: Se lo voy a mandar por correo.
english: I'm going to send it to him by mail.
tip: Sound rule: le + lo would sound awkward, so "le" becomes "se": "Se lo dije" (I told it to him), not "le lo dije."

target: Hablando del rey de Roma, mira quién viene.
english: Speaking of the devil, look who's coming.
tip: Where English summons the devil, Spanish summons 'el rey de Roma' – the king of Rome. Same magic: name someone and they appear. No actual royalty involved.

target: Me alegra que mis hijos sean tan responsables.
english: I'm glad that my children are so responsible.
tip: "Me alegra que" + subjunctive – expressing emotion about something.

target: Es una lástima que la tienda esté cerrando.
english: It is unfortunate that the shop is closing down.
tip: The shop really is closing – yet esté is subjunctive. Es una lástima que frames your reaction to a fact, and reactions take subjunctive even when the fact is true.

target: La sopa está fría, la voy a calentar.
english: The soup is cold, I'm going to heat it up.
tip: 'Está fría' – está flags a state the soup got into: it went cold, so you can fix it. 'Es fría' would describe gazpacho, cold by design and beyond rescuing.

target: Tarde o temprano, encontrarás la respuesta que buscas.
english: Sooner or later, you will find the answer you are looking for.
tip: Encontrarás is the true future tense – Spanish saves it for predictions and promises like this one, while everyday plans usually get voy a + verb.

target: Le tomé el pelo y se lo creyó todo.
english: I pulled his leg and he fell for it.
tip: English pulls legs; Spanish grabs hair: 'tomé el pelo' = I teased or fooled him. Different body part, same gentle deception.

target: Suspendí el examen de historia porque no estudié lo suficiente.
english: I failed the history exam because I didn't study enough.
tip: False friend alert: 'suspendí el examen' means I FAILED it, not postponed it. A suspended exam in Spain is a flunked one; to postpone, you want aplazar.

target: Si me lo hubieras pedido, te habría acompañado sin dudarlo.
english: If you had asked me, I would have accompanied you without hesitation.
tip: English says 'if you would have asked' – Spanish never puts conditional after si. The if-half takes 'hubieras pedido'; 'habría' lives only in the result half.

target: Sin que nadie nos lo advirtiera, terminamos en una zona peligrosa.
english: Without anyone warning us, we ended up in a dangerous area.
tip: "Sin que" (without) + subjunctive. Always triggers subjunctive.

target: Este sitio está en el quinto pino; tardamos una hora en llegar.
english: This place is in the middle of nowhere; it took us an hour to get there.
tip: 'El quinto pino' – the fifth pine – is Spanish for the middle of nowhere, after a real row of pines on old Madrid's edge; the fifth was a long hike out.

target: No es que no confíe en mis hijos, sino que me preocupo por ellos.
english: It's not that I don't trust my kids, but rather that I worry about them.
tip: No es que + subjunctive, sino que + indicative = it's not that... but rather...

target: Por muy inteligente que sea, necesita estudiar más.
english: However intelligent he may be, he needs to study more.
tip: Por muy + adjective + que + subjunctive = however much.

target: Dámelo, por favor.
english: Give it to me, please.
tip: Dámelo stacks da + me + lo in fixed order: person before thing, always me lo, never lo me. The written accent keeps the stress where plain da had it.
